findings.finding: The opening material does not rehearse finding a missing triangle angle or the complement of an angle in a right angle.
findings.breakdown: The elevation example uses the triangle angle sum; the depression example uses a partitioned right angle. Students must recall these calculations while learning the new angle references.
findings.checked: p3-identify rehearses classification, not missing-angle calculations. p4-finding-block states the relationships but provides no recall questions before the examples. No preceding topic is supplied or omitted. Recognising a right-angle marker alone is too elementary to retain as a substantial missing piece.
findings.assumptions: The angle relationships are prior learning from earlier years or Angle Relationships. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p3-information, add: (a) A right-angled triangle has another angle of 35°. Find the third angle. (55°.) (b) Repeat with 68°. (22°.) (c) A ray splits a right angle into 27° and y°. Find y. (63°.) (d) Repeat with 46°. (44°.) These four short items fit within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse both missing-angle calculations before the new definitions and examples, with the teacher checking responses.

findings.finding: Generalise the connection between an angle measured from the vertical and the paired elevation and depression angles.
findings.breakdown: The task connects complementary angles with equal alternate angles and asks students to explain when the given and calculated angles coincide.
findings.checked: p4-finding-block supplies both relationships, and p4-guided-block applies them. For an acute x, both requested angles are 90°−x°; equality with x° occurs at x=45°.

repair.proposal: After p5-q5, offer: A is below and left of B. AB makes an acute angle x° with the downward vertical at B. Draw horizontal reference lines through A and B. Express the elevation from A and depression from B in terms of x, explaining each relationship. When do both equal x°? Expected: depression=90°−x° by complementary angles; elevation=90°−x° by alternate angles; both equal x° when x=45°.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task requests explanations and includes the acute-angle condition.

findings.finding: The contextual trigonometry examples have no opening rehearsal of side identification, sine and tangent selection, inverse sine, or solving equations with an unknown numerator or denominator.
findings.breakdown: The kite example requires inverse sine, the flagpole example multiplies by an adjacent length, and the cliff example divides by a tangent. Students with recall gaps must recover these different operations while interpreting the contexts.
findings.checked: The preceding topic teaches elevation, depression and angle relationships, with no trigonometric calculations. Each retained prerequisite is used directly by a p6 worked example. Cosine is excluded because none of these examples uses it.
findings.assumptions: Right-Angled Trigonometry is prior course learning. Scientific calculators are available; calculator evaluation itself is not a missing review piece.

repair.proposal: Before p6-example-activity, add: (1) In triangle ABC with C=90° and reference angle at A, label AB, BC and AC as hypotenuse, opposite or adjacent; repeat with the reference angle at B. (2) Write the ratio equation for opposite 5 and hypotenuse 13, then for opposite 7 and adjacent 12. (3) Find θ to the nearest degree when sin θ=5/13. (4) Rearrange and find x to 1 d.p.: tan 35°=x/12 and tan 35°=12/x. Expected: H,O,A then H,A,O; sin θ=5/13 and tan θ=7/12; 23°; 8.4 and 17.1. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse the specific trigonometric decisions and equation forms used by the three examples before entering their contexts.

findings.finding: Compare one acute compass angle across all four quadrants.
findings.breakdown: Holding the acute angle constant exposes how the starting direction and direction of turn determine the true-bearing calculation.
findings.checked: Earlier true-bearing teaching models addition from south and subtraction from a full turn; p17 teaches compass conversion. The existing supplied practice does not hold one angle constant across four quadrants. All proposed conversions are correct.
findings.assumptions: The compass angle is acute and bearings are measured clockwise from north.

repair.proposal: After p17-guided, ask students to predict the quadrant of each true bearing before calculating. Convert (a) N30°E, (b) S30°E, (c) S30°W, (d) N30°W. Expected: 030°, 150°, 210°, 330°. The acute angle remains 30° while the quadrant changes. Follow with the unpatterned question: Convert S67°W to a true bearing. Expected: 247°.

findings.doneWhen: The optional run includes predictions, all four quadrants and the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: The reverse-bearing example uses cointerior angles without an opening rehearsal of identifying the pair and finding its missing angle.
findings.breakdown: The move from 64° at A to 116° at B depends on recognising same-side interior angles between parallel north references, a relationship not rehearsed by the immediately preceding topic.
findings.checked: Earlier p4 teaching supplies alternate angles, not cointerior angles. The preceding compass-bearing teaching and p19-q6 practise quadrant conversions and complements. p20 names cointerior angles in the worked captions but does not first ask students to recognise or calculate them.
findings.assumptions: Cointerior angles are prior learning from Angle Relationships. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p20-information-text, show two parallel vertical lines crossed by a sloping transversal and ask: (a) Mark a pair of cointerior angles. (b) One angle of a marked cointerior pair is 70°; find the other and name the relationship. (c) Repeat with 115°. Expected: a same-side interior pair; 110° and 65°, because cointerior angles sum to 180°. These three short items fit within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students identify and calculate cointerior angles before following the reverse-bearing example.

findings.finding: Seven complete bearing tasks are repeated without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Each later copy retains the same requested bearing, point arrangement, north references, angle location, angle direction and value. The repeats add no mathematical decision.
findings.checked: Compared the complete stems and question-diagram specifications for all seven pairs, excluding answer annotations. The pairs respectively repeat direct 105°, complementary reflex 255°, smaller angle 110° at B, smaller angle 70° at B, reverse bearing from reflex 280° at A, reverse bearing from clockwise 120° at B, and reverse bearing from clockwise 110° at A with one north reference. No explicit instructional purpose is supplied. Moving from guided practice to practice alone does not establish deliberate retrieval.
findings.assumptions: The supplied diagram specifications describe the original question givens. Changed labels, difficulty categories and answer annotations do not make the tasks distinct.

repair.proposal: Remove the later copies p23-q2-e, p23-q2-j, p23-q2-k, p24-q3-d, p24-q3-i, p24-q3-h and p26-q7a. Retain their earlier counterparts and all distinct tasks within the surrounding groups.

findings.doneWhen: Each of the seven unchanged tasks appears once, without deleting distinct parts or their shared instructions.

findings.finding: Explain the direct bearing for equal route legs, including a route whose bearings straddle north.
findings.breakdown: The extension uses the existing isosceles route structure to distinguish halfway around the shorter turn from averaging printed bearing numbers.
findings.checked: p30-q18 already asks students to use equal connected legs. Reverse bearings, triangle angle sums and equal base angles suffice. For 030° then 120°, the join angle is 90° and the direct bearing is 075°. For 350° then 010°, the join angle is 160° and the direct bearing is 000°.
findings.assumptions: Both legs have the same positive length. The proposed routes are nondegenerate.

repair.proposal: After p30-q18-d, offer: Two equal route legs have bearings 030° and 120°. Explain why the direct bearing from start to finish is 075° without measuring. Now use equal legs with bearings 350° and 010°: find the direct bearing and explain why averaging the printed numbers fails. Expected: the first route has a 90° join angle and 45° base angles, giving 075°. The second has a 160° join angle and 10° base angles, giving 000°. Its shorter turn passes through north; the numerical average 180° points south.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain both routes using the equal-leg triangle and identify the failure of ordinary numerical averaging across north.

findings.finding: The worked example labels and uses 30° without writing the decision that derives it from the given 060° bearing.
findings.breakdown: Students can reproduce the cosine substitution without seeing why the eastward component uses a 30° reference angle.
findings.checked: Step 1 supplies the 60° bearing; Step 2 introduces a 30° label; Step 3 substitutes it into cosine. Earlier complementary-angle teaching supplies the method but does not state this example's connecting calculation. The 30° is derived, not supplied directly by a standard diagram mark.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator is available for evaluating cosine; the finding concerns angle selection.

repair.proposal: Before the cosine equation, write: “The angle between east and AB is 90°−60°=30°.”

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly derives the angle used in its trigonometric equation.

findings.finding: The bearings-and-trigonometry topic does not rehearse identifying adjacent and hypotenuse, selecting cosine, or isolating an unknown numerator.
findings.breakdown: These prerequisites directly support choosing cos 30°=x/3 and obtaining x=3 cos 30°. The preceding topic practises bearing sketches and component labels without trigonometric equations.
findings.checked: p6 teaches earlier trigonometric applications, but it is separated from p33 by several bearing topics. The immediately preceding p32-q3 rehearses diagrams and horizontal and vertical distances, not ratio selection or rearrangement. The worked p33 example uses cosine specifically, so a review of all three ratios is unnecessary for this finding.
findings.assumptions: Right-Angled Trigonometry is prior course learning. Scientific calculators are available; evaluating cosine is excluded from the missing pieces.

repair.proposal: Before p33-method-block, add: (1) In triangle ABC with C=90° and reference angle at A, label AB, AC and BC as H, A or O; repeat with the reference angle at B. (2) Which ratio connects adjacent and hypotenuse? Write its formula. (3) Make x the subject of cos 35°=x/8. Expected: H,A,O then H,O,A; cos θ=A/H; x=8 cos 35°. Keep these short items within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse the side labels, cosine choice and rearrangement required by the worked example before applying them to bearings.

findings.finding: Hold journey length constant while comparing eastward and northward components across northeast bearings.
findings.breakdown: Students can connect a changing bearing with increasing eastward distance and decreasing northward distance, then transfer the method to another quadrant.
findings.checked: p6 supplies sine and cosine-related prior trigonometry assumptions; p33 demonstrates finding a component, and its guided questions use sine and cosine in different quadrants. The proposed component pairs are correct: 5.0/8.7, 7.1/7.1 and 8.7/5.0 km. The follow-up gives 10.6 km east and 7.5 km south.
findings.assumptions: Scientific calculators are available. Components are positive distances in their named directions.

repair.proposal: After p37-q9, offer: Before calculating, predict how eastward and northward distances change as the bearing increases. A walker travels 10 km on each bearing: 030°, 045°, 060°. Find both components to 1 d.p. and explain the pattern. Expected east/north pairs: 5.0/8.7, 7.1/7.1, 8.7/5.0 km. Journey length stays constant and only bearing varies. Follow with: A boat travels 13 km on bearing 125°. Find its eastward and southward components to 1 d.p. Expected: 10.6 km east and 7.5 km south.

findings.doneWhen: The optional sequence includes prediction, both components and an unpatterned southeast follow-up.
